claim: Real-world need for an item follows power laws of recency and frequency (exponents .73-.83 in three corpora), matching lab retention; this is the rationale for ACT-R base-level activation.
agent_test: Rank memories by ln(sum t^-d) vs recency-only vs exponential on a log of the agent's own past need events; compare hit rate at equal retrieved tokens.

claim: Power vs exponential forgetting form is not settled by data: Ebbinghaus replication fits both (power R2 .974, summed exp .995, AIC gap 2) and averaging artefacts can mimic power laws.
agent_test: Do not rely on the form; run both decays in an ablation on the same store and keep the one that wins on held-out recall.

claim: Spacing effect: spaced uses of an item raise later retrieval more than massed uses; ACT-R variant with activation-dependent decay fits 162 points (r2 .971) but misses chi-square (260 on 157 df).
agent_test: Compare spacing-aware scoring (decay slows with spaced reuse) to plain sum-of-powers on a multi-session memory benchmark.

claim: Stronger memories are not always forgotten more slowly: four sentence-recall replications and a visual STM study found starting level up, forgetting rate unchanged. This contradicts the ACT-R/Pavlik-Anderson idea that practice slows decay.
agent_test: Test a constant decay rate across use counts against use-count-dependent decay; if no difference, drop the extra parameter.

claim: Slowed clock: time between sessions counts for far less than clock time (H about 12 blocks per day); event count may be the better time variable than wall clock.
agent_test: Index decay by number of intervening memory events or turns rather than wall time, and compare at equal tokens.

claim: The dominant LLM-agent ranker (Generative Agents) is recency (exponential, 0.995 per hour since last retrieval) + importance (LLM 1-10) + relevance (cosine), min-max scaled, all weights 1. No frequency term; weights never tuned.
agent_test: Add a frequency/base-level term to the three-term score and compare retrieval accuracy at fixed top-k.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-10 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Generative Agents ablations remove whole modules (memory, reflection, planning), not retrieval terms; full architecture TrueSkill 29.89 vs 21.21 fully ablated. So no evidence isolates the value of any single retrieval term.
agent_test: Run the retrieval-term ablation Park et al. did not: drop recency, importance, relevance one at a time.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-10 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Ebbinghaus-style exponential strength with +1 per recall (MemoryBank) is used but its forgetting rule was never ablated against no forgetting.
agent_test: Ablate the forgetting rule in a MemoryBank-like store; measure correctness at equal prompt tokens.

claim: Recall-count-dependent decay beat Generative Agents scoring on 10 small tasks (paired t=-5.687, p=.0003) but tasks were built by the authors and both failed the habit-vs-one-off case. Task 0 detail: recall-count scoring picked the habitual event (University .850), Park scoring picked the recent one-off (Restaurant 1.620); both wrong.
agent_test: Replicate on an independent task set with a held-out habit/exception split.

claim: SYNAPSE (re-read this session) leads LoCoMo with GPT-4o-mini (F1 40.5 vs Zep 39.7, N=500, p<.05) and keeps its lead on GPT-4o (43.4 vs A-Mem 36.1) and Qwen-3b (36.6 vs 22.1). Its 'node decay' is a per-step propagation leak, not ACT-R base-level decay; removing it cuts temporal F1 50.1 to 14.2. Same authors, same benchmark, so benchmark generality is untested.
agent_test: Run the same graph on a benchmark where the older fact is sometimes right; do not cite as support for base-level decay.

claim: Retrieval method matters more than write method on LoCoMo (cosine 73.4% vs BM25 57.1%; hybrid+LLM rerank 77.2%); raw chunks match extracted memories. No recency or activation term was tested.
agent_test: Add base-level activation as a re-ranker on top of cosine; measure gain over cosine alone at fixed k.

claim: Forgetting and consolidation do not help on LongMemEval: aggressive consolidation 48.4% vs raw RAG 78.4% (S tier). Gains in the VSCode stream come mainly from deduplication, not decay.
agent_test: Never delete; use decay only to rank. Compare ranking-with-decay vs delete-with-decay at equal tokens.

claim: LoCoMo cannot test retention or decay: every query touches every memory, so decay weights saturate. Benchmarks need repeated use over time to test ACT-R-style frequency effects. CAMeR-Bench (76 memories, 100 rounds, graded query frequency) is the only use-history test found, and it scores weights, not answers.
agent_test: Build a small multi-session test where the right memory depends on use history.

claim: Decay-driven accessibility with reinforcement gives small accuracy gains but large token savings (OBLIVION 90.6% vs 89.0%, up to 73% cost cut) and its best temperature depends on buffer size.
agent_test: Measure tokens-to-correct-answer, not accuracy only.

claim: Embedding cosine can replace hand-set ACT-R association strengths: rho .50-.51 on semantic priming, but equal to plain regression, not better.
agent_test: Use embedding cosine as the spreading term; do not expect it to beat a tuned linear model.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-10 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: ACT-R parameters are weakly identified: noise and base-level constant vary across fitting methods; latency factor and activation mean trade off.
agent_test: Fix decay near 0.5 and tune only threshold; report sensitivity to d in {0.3,0.5,0.7}.

claim: ACT-R base-level plus spreading terms improve repeat-aware music recommendation (Last.fm NDCG 12.16%) where about 72-89% of test items are repeats; frequency alone fails on exploration (NDCG .07).
agent_test: Check what share of agent retrievals are repeats of earlier-used memories before adding use-history terms.

claim: Spaced reminders beat massed at high frequency in a 28-day field study (success .55 vs .38; N=64, cells 11-14), as a power-law activation model predicts.
agent_test: Not directly agent-relevant; informs scheduling of re-surfacing memory.

claim: Large-scale spaced-repetition data: modelled half-life regression cut MAE to .128 vs Leitner .235, but AUC is near chance (.538, Leitner .542), so calibration improves while item ranking does not.
agent_test: For ranking, test on AUC/NDCG, not calibration error.

claim: Biologically-inspired and spiking temporal retrieval (SynapticRAG) gained up to +14.66 points over RAG; ablating temporal integration cost -9.90 on average.
agent_test: Test a time-aware reranker on temporal questions.

claim: Human narrative recall depends on gist fit with the whole story, not just access history; no primacy effect in stories.
agent_test: Add a coherence-with-current-goal term next to activation.

claim: No paper found compares Park-style scoring head to head against true ACT-R base-level scoring on an LLM task. Honda 2025 exists (HAI '25, DOI 10.1145/3765766.3765803) but only its abstract was read: a simulation with no baseline and no numbers. Pensyve is still unverified.
agent_test: This is the core experiment: Park score vs ACT-R B+S vs hybrid at equal tokens.

claim: Existing LLM-memory papers each chose a different decay clock (game hours, wall seconds, turns since reinforcement, query rounds, timestamp gaps) and none compared clocks. The slowed-clock question is untested for agents.
agent_test: Replay one store with three clocks (wall, turns, intervening memory events) and compare NDCG.

claim: No LLM-memory paper tests power-law against exponential decay at ranking. Designs use exponential (OBLIVION, CAMeR, Park) or a hand-set stretched exponential (FadeMem beta .8/1.2). In humans the best Bayesian study (Averell & Heathcote 2011) fits individuals with an exponential yet selects a power function by Bayesian comparison.
agent_test: Fit both forms on the agent's own reuse log; pick by held-out NDCG, not by prior.

claim: On a habitual slot with a one-off exception (Hou Task 0), frequency scoring picks the habit and recency scoring picks the latest one-off; both fail. Neither term alone handles exceptions.
agent_test: Add a goal or explicit-statement term; test on a set of exceptions announced by the user.

claim: No study compares rank-by-activation without deletion against delete-on-decay at equal tokens. OBLIVION never ablates decay on versus off; Kerestecioglu's gain came from deduplication; time-driven decay alone collapses weights to near zero (CAMeR).
agent_test: Same store, same budget: rank-only vs delete vs neither, on a replay with repeated use.

claim: Counting every retrieval as a use probably reinforces passenger memories: in an ALFWorld audit only 5.9% of retrieval-credited successes were marginal helps (abstract only).
agent_test: Increment use count only when the final answer cites the memory; compare with count-on-retrieval.

claim: Sensitivity of decay settings is modest but real and noisy. SYNAPSE delta 0.3/0.5/0.7 gives 40.0/40.5/38.1 avg F1. OBLIVION temperature results are non-monotone and the text's best value (T=10) disagrees with the table at buffer 60 (T=1 highest).
agent_test: Report results at d in {0.3, 0.5, 0.7} with repeated seeds; ignore differences below the seed noise.

claim: The smallest use-history benchmark that exists is CAMeR-Bench (76 memories, 100 rounds, query counts 0 to 37), which scores weights not answers; MemoryAgentBench tests overwrite, not frequency. A usable test needs answer-level scoring with graded reuse and some exceptions.
agent_test: Build 100 to 200 questions on about 80 memories over 20 sessions with graded reuse, one-off exceptions and stale facts.

claim: Gains of a few points on LoCoMo-sized sets are within noise: BM25 vs full context at n=160 gave p=0.09 for a 8.8 point gap; a power analysis put confirmation at about 360 to 430 questions.
agent_test: Size any retrieval-term test at 400+ questions or paired replays.
